module_descriptions.br-01: Start with the idea that a sentence is made of groups of words nested inside larger groups. You’ll learn to use a tree to show which words belong together and how one branch can contain an entire phrase.
module_descriptions.br-02: Look at the first split in a basic sentence to see how the subject and predicate fit together. You’ll distinguish the kind of phrase you’re looking at from the job it does in the sentence.
module_descriptions.br-03: Explore how the head of a phrase gives the phrase its category. Using adjective phrases, you’ll see how an adjective can stand on its own or combine with a degree word such as “very.”
module_descriptions.br-04: Study how the complements a verb takes shape the verb phrase. You’ll build a basic transitive VP and see how the verb and its direct object fit together inside it.
module_descriptions.br-05: Compare a verb’s complement with an adverbial that adds detail to the action. You’ll build two levels of VP and see how the point where an adverbial attaches changes the structure.
module_descriptions.br-06: Examine what happens to a verb phrase when a helping verb is added. You’ll build a progressive construction and see how the auxiliary heads a larger VP that contains the main verb phrase.
module_descriptions.br-07: Look inside a noun phrase to see how a determiner and a nominal work together. You’ll use DET and NOM to represent a simple phrase with a demonstrative and a noun.
module_descriptions.br-08: See how a clause can sit inside a larger sentence. You’ll use a clause beginning with “that” to show where the complementiser sits and how it connects to the embedded subject and predicate.
module_descriptions.br-09: Follow the changes that turn a statement into an object question. You’ll track where the wh-word and auxiliary appear at the front and how the tree represents the positions they leave behind.
module_descriptions.br-10: Explore how infinitival “to” fits into a verb phrase without carrying tense. You’ll distinguish it from the preposition “to” and see how it combines with a verb in its base form.
module_descriptions.br-11: Consider why listing sentences can never capture everything speakers can say. You’ll see how a finite set of grammar rules can describe the structure of sentences you’ve never encountered before.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch01: Learn why a contraction such as we’re cannot stand for a whole coordinated subject, and how to write the pair clearly.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch03: This module explains verb forms and auxiliaries in plain English, with examples that show how the pattern works in a whole sentence and how to choose the right form when you write.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch04: Learn how each verb chooses the phrases that follow it, how objects and pronouns take their places, and how to repair the mistakes that come from giving a verb the wrong company.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch05: This module explains nouns and determiners in plain English, with examples that show how the pattern works in a whole sentence and how to choose the right form when you write.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch06: Learn where enough goes and why accustomed to is followed by an -ing form.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch07: Learn where ago goes and how to join a time clause with before.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch10: Learn how questions, imperatives, tags and exclamations are built, and where each small word belongs.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch13: Learn how to compare two things, how to rank one thing in a larger set, and which small words go with each pattern.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch14: Learn how to build clauses without tense: for-infinitivals, object-plus-infinitive patterns, auxiliary order, bare and to-infinitives, and -ing modifiers.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch15: Learn how to keep coordinated pieces parallel and how to anchor a describing clause to the noun it describes.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch16: Learn how English moves objects, uses clefts and chooses passive frames to put information where it fits best.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch17: This module explains pronouns and pro-forms in plain English, with examples that show how the pattern works in a whole sentence and how to choose the right form when you write.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch18: Learn the spelling changes that happen when words take endings, and two small patterns for plurals, possessives and articles.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch19: Learn how compounds, prefixes, ordinals and fractions are written and how their endings change.
module_descriptions.cgel-ch20: Learn how to mark sentence boundaries, join clauses, quote speech and handle apostrophes, hyphens and abbreviations.

options.feedback: “The clock” names only the subject. Include what happened to it.
“Sol realised” belongs to the main clause. The embedded clause begins at that.
The content clause includes its marker, subject and predicate.

predict.prompt: Which stretch is the embedded clause in “Sol realised that the clock had stopped”?
predict.hint: First find the complete stretch that tells you what Sol realised.

options.text: The caretaker has gone still gives the content of believe.
options.feedback: The clause has its own subject and predicate and functions as the complement of believe.

options.text: The word I sets off a separate sentence.
options.feedback: Has is a verb within the clause. Include the caretaker and the rest of the predicate.

options.text: The word has is itself an embedded clause.
options.feedback: I is the main subject. The whole report is still one written sentence.

guided.prompt: In “I believe the caretaker has gone”, why is there an embedded clause even though that is absent?
guided.hint: Read “the caretaker has gone” by itself. Which verb gives it a job in the longer sentence?

options.feedback: The second sentence has one clause, but the first has both the noticing and the observation.
A clause nested inside a sentence does not have its own written boundary.
The first sentence contains a main clause and an embedded clause. The second contains one clause.

transfer.prompt: In “Mina noticed the kettle was boiling. She switched it off”, how many written sentences and clauses are there?
transfer.hint: Count the written boundaries first. Then look for a clause inside the first sentence.

options.feedback: But links ideas inside the one written sentence.

options.text: One sentence with two coordinated clauses, one containing an embedded clause
options.feedback: But coordinates Mira knew the gate was stuck with Jo tried the handle. The gate was stuck is embedded inside the first coordinate.

options.text: One sentence whose three clauses are all coordinates
options.feedback: The gate was stuck gives the content of knew, so it sits inside the first coordinate.

exit.prompt: Which analysis fits “Mira knew the gate was stuck, but Jo tried the handle”?
exit.hint: Underline what but joins, then see whether either side contains a clause of its own.

key_terms.definition: A unit of text. In ordinary prose, an initial capital and a terminal mark usually help identify its boundaries.
A grammatical unit organised around a predicate. A typical finite clause has its own subject and predicate.
A clause that serves as part of a larger construction, for example as the complement of a verb.
The joining of units at the same structural level, often with a word such as and or but.

outcomes.text: Find the full subject before deciding whether to contract a form of be.
Distinguish coordinated noun phrases from coordinated clauses.
Explain why contractions are possible in some sentences that contain and.

teaching.text: Read “You are on the list” and “Maya and you are on the list” aloud. Ask the learner to bracket the subject before trying the reduction.
Keep the target to contraction with a coordinated subject ending in a pronoun. Contractions with other kinds of subject are a separate question.

worked_example.sentence: I’m at the desk, and you’re at the door.

steps.text: Expand the contractions to expose “I am” and “you are”.
Locate the two predicates, “am at the desk” and “are at the door”.
Each pronoun is the whole subject of its own clause, so both reductions work.

key_terms.definition: A reduced form written with an apostrophe, as in you’re for you are.
One subject made up of coordinated expressions, as in Maya and you.
The shortening of a form such as are to ’re and its attachment to the preceding word.

options.feedback: “You are” includes are, which starts the predicate. Start earlier and stop just before are.
Rae is one member of the subject. The waiting applies to both Rae and you.
Both names belong to the one subject of are waiting.

predict.prompt: In “Rae and you are waiting”, which words tell us who is waiting?
predict.hint: Find the complete answer to “Who is waiting?”

options.text: I and you are on the rota.
options.feedback: The coordinated subject takes the full form are in this wording.

options.text: I and you is on the rota.
options.feedback: Is would fit a single third-person subject. The coordinated subject here uses are.

options.text: I and you’re on the rota.
options.feedback: You is only one member of that subject. Give the whole pair the full form are.

guided.prompt: The intended subject is “I and you”. Choose the ordinary form for the single shared predicate.
guided.hint: Expand ’re and read the subject and verb separately.

options.text: Mira is on the early shift, and you’re on it too.
options.feedback: The first version gives Mira and you separate predicates, so you’re is available.

options.text: Mira and you’re on the early shift.
options.feedback: This still tries to contract the verb after one coordinated subject. Give Mira a complete clause.

options.text: Mira and you are both on the early shift.
options.feedback: The wording is grammatical, but Mira and you still share a single predicate.

transfer.prompt: Choose a two-clause version of “Mira and you are on the early shift”.
transfer.hint: Give Mira a predicate of her own before and.

options.text: Needed must always follow the full are.
options.feedback: Needed can follow ’re when “you” is the whole subject, as the first line shows.

options.text: The time phrase blocks all contraction.
options.feedback: At eight is present in both lines. The difference is the boundary around the subject.

options.text: In the first, you is the whole subject. In the second it is a coordinate within the subject.
options.feedback: The contrast comes from the subject boundary. The time phrase and the participle are present in both.

exit.prompt: Why is “At eight, you’re needed” natural but “At eight, Jo and you’re needed” unsuitable for one shared predicate?
exit.hint: Compare how much of the line counts as the subject in each case.

outcomes.text: Choose an auxiliary for an ordinary negative or question, including when do is needed.
Build an auxiliary chain in order and select the verb form required at each step.
Explain selected differences in tense, aspect and modal interpretation in context.

teaching.text: Ask which verb would move if the sentence became a question. A lexical verb such as “checks” cannot fill that slot on its own in the ordinary construction, so “does” enters and “check” loses the tense ending.
Work from left to right through long verb chains. When two links have the same spelling, use the form they select to decide what job each link is doing.
Ask learners to supply the situation for a tense answer. A finished time, a period continuing to now and a past reporting viewpoint give different reasons for the same visible verb forms.

worked_example.sentence: Has the new valve been tested?

steps.text: Put the subject first to recover “The new valve has been tested”.
Identify “has” as the perfect auxiliary and “been” as its past-participle complement.
Identify “been” as passive be because it selects “tested”. In the question only “has” precedes the subject.

key_terms.definition: A verb that can fill special grammatical roles, such as carrying negation or appearing before the subject in a question.
The use of auxiliary do when a construction needs an auxiliary and the clause lacks a suitable one.
The uninflected verb form used after modal auxiliaries and supportive do, as in check.
A verb form used in constructions such as has checked, was checked or is checking.
A tense choice in an embedded report that takes the original occasion of speaking as a reference point.

options.text: Nina not has checked the seal.
options.feedback: Not follows the finite auxiliary in this ordinary clause.

options.text: Nina has not checked the seal.
options.feedback: The auxiliary has is present and can carry not without do-support.

options.text: Nina does not have checked the seal.
options.feedback: Have in the affirmative is already an auxiliary here. Keep it in the negative.

predict.prompt: Change “Nina has checked the seal” to a straightforward negative.
predict.hint: Look for a verb already capable of carrying not.

options.text: Was is passive, and being is perfect.
options.feedback: Was is followed by an -ing form, the signature of the progressive. Perfect have is absent.

options.text: Both forms of be are progressive.
options.feedback: Being selects checked, a past participle. That is the passive link.

options.text: Was is progressive, and being is passive.
options.feedback: Progressive was selects being. Passive being selects checked and makes the affected seal the subject.

guided.prompt: What is the role of be in “The seal was being checked”?
guided.hint: Look at what each form of be selects next.

options.text: If the valve will leak, we stopped the test.
options.feedback: The clause is about a hypothetical response. The two tenses here do not express that reading together.

options.text: If the valve leaked, we would stop the test.
options.feedback: The preterite presents the condition as remote, and would marks the consequence in this construction.

options.text: If the valve leaked, we stop the test.
options.feedback: The present stop does not express the ordinary remote consequence. Use the modal that matches the remote condition.

transfer.prompt: Which best presents a response to a hypothetical leak in the remote construction taught here?
transfer.hint: Read the condition and the consequence as one hypothetical pair.

options.text: Rae managed to lift the hatch.
options.feedback: Managed to reports an achievement. The other examples express past ability and future possibility.

options.text: Rae could lift the hatch as a child.
options.feedback: This says Rae had the ability, and leaves open whether she used it on a particular occasion.

options.text: Rae might lift the hatch tomorrow.
options.feedback: This is about a future possibility. It gives no report of a completed lift.

exit.prompt: Which wording explicitly says Rae succeeded once in her attempt to lift the hatch?
exit.hint: Distinguish having an ability from using it successfully on one occasion.

outcomes.text: Identify the complement a particular verb and sense allow.
Distinguish an object, a prepositional complement and an optional adjunct.
Preserve the correct verb frame when adding recipients, particles or pronouns.

teaching.text: Use a single meaning across several verbs, such as informing a visitor. Have the learner test “tell the visitor the result”, “explain the result to the visitor” and “say what happened”.
Optionality is a clue about a dependent, but a verb can license a complement without requiring it on every occasion. Also check whether the verb keeps its sense when the words are removed.

worked_example.sentence: We sent her the checklist, then switched the lamp off.

steps.text: Identify “her” as the recipient and “the checklist” as the thing sent.
Use “sent the checklist to her” as another frame available to send.
Replace “the lamp” with “it” and place the pronoun before off.

key_terms.definition: The set of complement patterns available to a word in a particular sense.
A dependent whose type or presence is licensed by the head of its construction.
An added dependent specifying circumstances such as time, place or manner.
A short word such as back or off that forms a construction with a verb and may alternate in position with a noun-phrase object.

options.feedback: Consist uses of. Depend selects a different preposition.
Depend selects on in this frame.
Depend does not take the available parts as a bare object in this sense.

predict.prompt: What can complete “The repair depends ___ the parts available”?
predict.hint: Keep the verb depend and look for the preposition it selects.

options.text: They enjoy that fixing old lamps.
options.feedback: That could introduce a finite clause, but the words after it do not form one here.

options.text: They enjoy to fix old lamps.
options.feedback: A to-infinitival is available after tend. Enjoy selects a different activity complement.
Enjoy can take the gerund-participial clause fixing old lamps.

guided.prompt: Which sentence uses the ordinary activity complement for enjoy?
guided.hint: Compare the complement endings in tends to fix and enjoys fixing.

options.text: She handed he the lamp and then switched off it.
options.feedback: He is nominative and cannot fill the recipient slot here. The unstressed it also needs to precede off.

options.text: Her handed him the lamp and then switched it off.
options.feedback: The particle frame has been fixed. The finite subject still needs nominative she.

options.text: She handed him the lamp and then switched it off.
options.feedback: The finite subject is nominative she, him is the object, and unstressed it precedes off.

transfer.prompt: Choose the edit for “Her handed him the lamp and then switched off it.”
transfer.hint: Check the subject and recipient first. Then put the small object pronoun beside the particle verb.

options.text: A complement always appears before the verb.
options.feedback: Complement position varies. Look at what the verb licenses in the relevant sense.

options.text: The complement is permitted by the particular verb and sense. The time adjunct adds a circumstance.
options.feedback: A verb may license an optional complement, so its licensing is a better first clue than whether you can omit it.

options.text: Every complement is obligatory, and every adjunct is a clause.
options.feedback: Some complements can be left out, such as the object of read. The licensing test covers both optional and obligatory cases.

exit.prompt: What distinguishes a licensed complement from a time adjunct in these examples?
exit.hint: Ask which dependent the verb specifically makes room for.

outcomes.text: Build noun phrases with determiners suited to the meaning and number of the noun.
Recognise when a determiner or modifier can do the work of a missing head.
Find the relevant noun phrase when choosing pronoun case or verb agreement.

teaching.text: Contrast a number as a total with a number of as a quantifying construction. Let the learner explain what the sentence is about before choosing between is and are.
Start a determiner exercise with a pair the learner can hold fixed, such as each lantern and every lantern. Then remove lantern and ask what has to return to the phrase.

worked_example.sentence: The number of lamps is falling, but a number of lanterns are still available.

steps.text: In the first clause, “the number” refers to a total, so choose singular “is”.
In the second clause, “a number of lanterns” means several lanterns, so choose plural “are”.
Check the reading of each noun phrase before looking at the noun immediately beside the verb.

key_terms.definition: The central word around which a phrase is built, such as lantern in the old lantern near the door.
A function in a noun phrase. A determiner can indicate which things are meant or how many there are.
Count uses treat things as individual units. Mass uses present material or a collection without counting units directly.
A construction in which one expression does the work of the head as well as another function, as each does in each was labelled.
The relation that gives us forms such as the box is and the boxes are.

options.text: The police are here. The news is good.
options.feedback: Police has plural agreement, while news has singular agreement despite its ending.

options.text: The police are here. The news are good.
options.feedback: The police half is right. News takes singular agreement despite its ending.

options.text: The police is here. The news are good.
options.feedback: Police uses plural agreement in the ordinary collective reference, while news is singular.

predict.prompt: Which pair combines ordinary agreements?
predict.hint: Treat police and news as two separate tests of head number.

options.feedback: Were supplies a verb, but the gap needs a noun-like head to go with every.
Every cannot carry the head function alone in this construction. One supplies the head.
Them cannot be the head immediately after every. Compare “every one of them”.

guided.prompt: Finish the remark about three labelled lanterns. “I inspected every lantern. Every ___ was safe.”
guided.hint: Try saying “every lantern” and then replacing lantern with a general count word.

options.text: three hundred blankets / hundreds of blankets
options.feedback: The exact numeral uses uninflected hundred. The approximate plural noun takes an of phrase.

options.text: three hundred of blankets / hundreds blankets
options.feedback: Remove of from the exact numeral and include it after plural hundreds in the approximate phrase.

options.text: three hundreds blankets / hundred of blankets
options.feedback: An exact count keeps hundred uninflected, while an approximate plural uses hundreds of.

transfer.prompt: Which pair distinguishes an exact count from an approximate large quantity?
transfer.hint: Check whether the number phrase states a precise count or describes a broad quantity.

options.feedback: Her and he reverse the expected cases, and “keys” is inside the of phrase, leaving box as the head that controls agreement.
She works as subject. The recipient needs him, and the second verb agrees with box.
She is the subject, him the recipient object, and the head box controls singular agreement.

exit.prompt: Which version keeps the cases and agreement in “___ gave ___ the box of keys. The box of keys ___ heavy.”?
exit.hint: Find the giver, the recipient and the head of the second subject.

outcomes.text: Place enough according to the expression it modifies.
Recognise prepositional to after accustomed and contrast it with infinitival to.
Explain the choices in a sentence that contains both constructions.

teaching.text: Try “enough light” beside “bright enough” before introducing category names. Ask what would need to increase for each statement to become true.
Keep “accustomed to the schedule” on screen as the learner changes schedule to an activity. The preposition remains in place.

worked_example.sentence: The crew checked the wiring enough to trust it.

steps.text: Find the extent being measured, namely the checking.
Keep “the wiring” immediately after its verb and let “enough” follow the short object.
Read “to trust it” as the threshold reached by the amount of checking.

key_terms.definition: How far a quality or activity reaches, as in bright enough.
The to in accustomed to the schedule or accustomed to working late.
The to before a plain verb in an infinitival clause, as in to work late.

options.feedback: Bright names a quality and is graded by a following enough. The other examples measure amounts.
Here enough specifies a quantity of light. The exercise asks for a quality graded by enough.
Lamps are counted or quantified. Look for a word describing how bright something is.

predict.prompt: Choose the natural comparison that contains an adjective phrase followed by enough.
predict.hint: Decide whether the example measures an amount or grades a quality.

options.feedback: A finite clause with they take does not fit right after that preposition.
To is a preposition after accustomed, and taking introduces its activity complement.
Take is a plain form. Prepositional to after accustomed takes an activity form in -ing.

guided.prompt: Choose the complement that fits “They grew accustomed to ___ the first flight.”
guided.hint: Try “accustomed to the journey” to identify the kind of to.

options.text: We’re accustomed to play outside but haven’t practised the ending enough.
options.feedback: The position of enough is right. The activity after accustomed to needs playing.

options.text: We’re accustomed to playing outside but haven’t practised the ending enough.
options.feedback: Use playing after prepositional to. Put enough after the direct object.

options.text: We’re accustomed to playing outside but haven’t enough practised the ending.
options.feedback: Playing fits after accustomed to. For extent, put enough after the short object the ending.

transfer.prompt: Revise “We’re accustomed to play outside but haven’t practised enough the ending.”
transfer.hint: Work on the part after accustomed separately from the part after practised.

options.text: Jo is accustomed to staying late to finish the mix.
options.feedback: The first to in the correct line heads a preposition phrase. The second introduces an infinitival of purpose.

options.text: Jo is accustomed to the late shift and to the noise.
options.feedback: Both instances are prepositions before noun phrases. Look for one serving another job.

options.text: Jo plans to stay late to finish the mix.
options.feedback: Both instances introduce infinitivals here, as the plain verbs stay and finish show.

exit.prompt: Which sentence uses two different kinds of to?
exit.hint: Look at the word immediately after each to and at what introduced it.

outcomes.text: Identify what can follow before and related prepositions introducing clauses.
Put ago and elapsed-time on after the duration phrase.
Distinguish backward counting from the present from forward counting from an earlier event.

teaching.text: Treat “before the alarm” and “before the alarm sounded” as a pair. Ask what comes after before in each and have the learner test the effect of inserting that in the clause.
Write the date of the telling above the date of the event. Draw the two offsets in words before asking a learner to turn them into an ago or on phrase.

worked_example.sentence: They checked the tide before the team left. Three weeks on, they checked it again.

steps.text: Find “the team left”, the clause licensed by “before”.
Read “three weeks on” as a forward step from the earlier occasion in the account.
Keep the duration “three weeks” before “on”.

key_terms.definition: A word that heads a preposition phrase. In the Cambridge analysis it can take a noun phrase or clause as complement, among other possibilities.
A clause such as the siren rang, which can serve as a complement inside a larger construction.
The time from which an expression counts backward or forward.

options.text: We moved before did the siren ring.
options.feedback: The clause after before keeps subject–verb order. It is not phrased as a direct question.

options.text: We moved after the siren rang.
options.feedback: After reverses the time relation given in the original line.

options.text: We moved before the siren rang.
options.feedback: Removing that preserves both the events and their time relation.

predict.prompt: Which version leaves the events in the same order and repairs “We moved before that the siren rang”?
predict.hint: Hold the order of the events fixed. Change only the string after before.

options.text: three days ago / three days on
options.feedback: Both ago and elapsed-time on follow their duration complement.

options.text: ago three days / three days on
options.feedback: The first expression puts ago on the wrong side of the duration.

options.text: three days ago / on three days
options.feedback: The ago phrase works. Use the same duration-first order with elapsed-time on.

guided.prompt: Which pair puts the duration on the correct side in both constructions?
guided.hint: Read the duration as a single phrase before looking at the head.

options.feedback: The report date is used for ago. On measures from the event it just established.
That would be one year before the 2020 closure. On counts forward.
Ago places the closure in 2020. On measures forward one year from the closure.

transfer.prompt: Written in 2026: “The hall closed six years ago. One year on, the work began.” When did the work begin?
transfer.hint: Use the date of the report for ago and the closure for on.

options.text: Both heads must come before the dependent.
options.feedback: Ago shows that a head can follow its dependent in these expressions.

options.text: Before precedes its clause. Ago follows its duration and counts back from the present.
options.feedback: Before and ago head time phrases with different complement types and different orders.

options.text: Ago introduces a clause just as before does.
options.feedback: Before takes a clause here. Ago goes with the duration phrase five years.

exit.prompt: Which explanation distinguishes “before the siren rang” from “five years ago”?
exit.hint: Identify the type and position of the dependent in each phrase.

outcomes.text: Choose clause order for an ordinary direct question or its embedded counterpart.
Recognise special question patterns and form response-seeking tags.
Distinguish a command, an exclamation and a question by their grammar.

teaching.text: Use quoted dialogue to distinguish what a speaker is doing from the form they choose. A declarative “You’re leaving?” can request confirmation even with unchanged word order.
In long examples, draw the boundary of the embedded question before deciding where inversion belongs. The edge of the written sentence is too broad a guide.

worked_example.sentence: Do you know which of the drawers Rowan checked?

steps.text: Identify “Do you know …?” as the main closed interrogative.
Keep “which of the drawers” together as one interrogative phrase inside it.
Read “Rowan checked” in ordinary order within the subordinate question.

key_terms.definition: A question clause with a limited set of answers, typically yes or no.
A question clause that asks for missing information, commonly with who, what, where or how.
A short auxiliary-and-pronoun question attached to a clause, as in aren’t they?
A clause type commonly used for instructions, with a plain-form verb and often an understood subject.

options.feedback: “How many” gives the quantity expression, but the fronted group includes the things counted.
How by itself does not express the question that “three spare keys” would answer.
The full phrase, including spare keys, asks for the quantity and functions as the object of find.

predict.prompt: What is the whole fronted question phrase in “How many spare keys did you find?”
predict.hint: Read the full phrase that could be answered with “three spare keys”.

options.feedback: The main clause inverts do and you. The embedded question retains subject–verb order.
Only the first clause is a direct question. Look at you and know in the larger clause.
Where the bus stops preserves subject–verb order.

guided.prompt: In “Do you know where the bus stops?”, where is the ordinary question inversion?
guided.hint: Find the question that is being asked directly.

options.feedback: The closed interrogative licenses this use of any. The positive declarative with some normally asks for confirmation.
This is a declarative confirmation pattern, which lacks the ordinary licensing for this use of any.
Some is ordinary in this declarative confirmation. The task asks for the neutral question with any.

transfer.prompt: Which question asks neutrally whether there were keys, using polarity-sensitive any?
transfer.hint: Compare a neutral question with a request to confirm an assumption.

options.text: Jo told us not open it.
options.feedback: Not belongs before the entire to-infinitival. Keep the marker to.

options.text: Jo told us to don’t open it.
options.feedback: Supportive do belongs in the direct imperative. The report uses an infinitival with not.

options.text: Jo told us not to open it.
options.feedback: The infinitival puts not before to. Do-support belongs to the direct negative imperative.

exit.prompt: How does “Don’t open it” become an infinitival report after “Jo told us”?
exit.hint: Check where not goes in a reported infinitival.

outcomes.text: Recover the missing counterpart in a comparative clause and decide when a subject is needed.
Select the expression and complement that convey the intended comparison.
Distinguish a ranking in a noun phrase from a free superlative.

teaching.text: Ask learners to name the two properties or quantities before filling a comparative blank. They can then see why “very” competes for the degree the construction supplies.
For superlatives, identify whether there is a head noun and state the comparison set aloud. That distinguishes “the lowest price” from “the lowest it has been”.

worked_example.sentence: The new drawer opens more quietly than the old one did.

steps.text: Name the property being compared, the quietness of the opening.
In the comparative clause, “did” stands for the opening and “the old one” is its subject.
Try the shorter “than the old one” and observe that this time there is no retained verb.

key_terms.definition: The clause in a comparison such as than it was or as it is wide, with part of its interpretation supplied by the larger construction.
The group of things or occasions a ranking is made over.
A form such as deepest or most efficiently, used to locate the extreme of a scale within a set.

options.text: Mira works harder than she worked hard last year.
options.feedback: This repeats the degree description and drops did. Keep did with a subject.

options.text: Mira works harder than she did last year.
options.feedback: The instruction calls for keeping did, so insert she. The version without did is also grammatical but uses a shorter construction.

options.text: Mira works harder than last year.
options.feedback: This is grammatical but removes did, which the question asks you to retain.

predict.prompt: Which edit keeps the same subject and the comparative verb in “Mira works harder than did last year”?
predict.hint: Keep did and ask who was working last year.

options.feedback: The ordinary quantity word with mass hardware is less.
Brackets works with fewer. Hardware is a mass noun in this use.
Fewer is the ordinary choice here for individual brackets. Less measures the amount of hardware.

guided.prompt: Which pair distinguishes a count of parts from an amount of material?
guided.hint: Decide which noun names individual items and which names an amount.

options.feedback: This identifies a room by how it ranks among rooms. Nothing tracks its earlier noise levels.

options.text: The room is the quietest it has ever been.
options.feedback: The free superlative and integrated clause set the comparison across occasions in the same room.

options.text: This is the quietest room here.
options.feedback: This ranks rooms against each other. The question asks about occasions in the same room.

transfer.prompt: Which version compares the present noise level with all earlier ones?
transfer.hint: Compare different rooms with different occasions in the same room.

options.text: The degree position that the comparison already supplies
options.feedback: The clause needs to leave the degree of width for the construction to interpret.
It supplies the subject of the second clause. Very goes with wide instead.

options.text: The position of the adjective wide itself
options.feedback: Wide names the property under comparison. Very would specify its degree independently.

exit.prompt: What would very occupy in “as deep as it is very wide”?
exit.hint: Try asking “to what degree wide?”

outcomes.text: Identify the expressed or understood subject of a non-finite clause.
Choose the form of the infinitival in active, passive and interrogative constructions.
Apply auxiliary order and recognise a participial modifier without adding a relative marker.

teaching.text: Ask learners to name the person doing the lower action separately from the grammatical position of that person’s expression. The answers need not use the same label.
When comparing an active and passive with make, keep the lower activity fixed. The appearance of to is easier to see when the rest stays familiar.

worked_example.sentence: The engineer asked which valve to open.

steps.text: Keep “which valve” together as the interrogative phrase.
Interpret it as the object of “open”. The subject is understood from context.
To make the intended actor explicit, choose a finite question such as “which valve the trainee should open”.

key_terms.definition: A clause whose verb is an infinitival or participial form, as in to check the gauge or checking the gauge.
An infinitival with a plain-form verb and without the marker to.
A subject present as words in the clause, as him is in for him to speak.

options.feedback: He is nominative. In this infinitival with for, the subject takes the accusative form.
The subject of the for-infinitival is accusative him.
His is genitive. The for-infinitival in this exercise requires him.

predict.prompt: After “We waited for ___ to answer”, which pronoun names the one person expected to answer?
predict.hint: Find the subject inside the infinitival, then test its case.

options.feedback: The lower verb belongs in an infinitival. The past marking is already carried by were.
Start would fit the active causative. The passive requires a different form.
The passive construction changes the bare infinitival of the active into a to-infinitival.

guided.prompt: Make the lower event accurate in “The trainees were made ___ again.”
guided.hint: Begin with the active “They made the trainees start”, and change the higher verb to passive.

options.feedback: Which door supplies the object. The action is to open that door.

options.text: Whether the words form a question
options.feedback: Which door makes the subordinate clause interrogative. What the clause leaves out is the person doing the opening.
Which door supplies the object. The actor is left to context.

transfer.prompt: In “We asked which door to open”, what is left understood?
transfer.hint: Which door already identifies what is opened.

options.text: The first needs who before waiting.
options.feedback: Holding or waiting can directly modify a noun. Use who when you choose a finite relative such as who is waiting.

options.text: The first has a participial modifier. The second has a finite relative.
options.feedback: Waiting outside has no tense-bearing auxiliary. Who is waiting outside is finite.

options.text: Both have expressed subjects inside their modifiers.
options.feedback: The subject is understood in the participial modifier. The relative marker represents it in the finite version.

exit.prompt: How does “the guest waiting outside” differ from “the guest who is waiting outside”?
exit.hint: Compare the versions for a finite auxiliary and a relative marker.

outcomes.text: Test whether two proposed coordinates can serve the same function in context.
Recognise restrictions on coordinating clause forms and nouns under one determiner.
Trace a supplementary relative clause to its anchor.

teaching.text: Give learners two expressions that each work alone as subject, then invite them to coordinate them. This surfaces why functional equivalence is only the first check.
When removing a supplementary relative for comparison, keep its anchor in the sentence. Read the remaining clause aloud and then restore the comment.

worked_example.sentence: The crate was sturdy and in good condition, which reassured the curator.

steps.text: Check that “sturdy” and “in good condition” each work after “was”.
Read the relative as a comment on the preceding state of affairs.
Keep the comma to distinguish the supplement from the coordinated descriptions.

key_terms.definition: One member of a pair or series joined at the same structural level.
An expression set apart from the main structure that adds information about an anchor.
The expression, person, thing or situation a supplement comments on.

options.text: They arrived yesterday and in the lobby.
options.feedback: In the lobby can fill the location-adjunct slot. The bare noun phrase cannot do so here.

options.text: The lobby and they arrived yesterday.
options.feedback: Making the lobby a subject changes the meaning. Keep it in the location phrase.

options.text: They arrived yesterday but the lobby.
options.feedback: But no longer joins equivalent adjuncts if “the lobby” stays bare.

predict.prompt: What small grammatical change repairs “They arrived yesterday and the lobby”?
predict.hint: Give the location a form that can follow arrived by itself.

options.text: To label the crates or photographing them would help.
options.feedback: This mixes an infinitival and an -ing clause in one coordination.

options.text: To label the crates or to photograph them would help.
options.feedback: Both coordinates in the first option have to-infinitival form. The last option works grammatically but switches both forms.

options.text: Labelling the crates or photographing them would help.
options.feedback: Both clauses here are gerund-participial. The task asks for the pair with to-infinitivals.

guided.prompt: Which revision keeps both proposed activities in infinitival form?
guided.hint: Keep the subject coordination but check both verb forms.

options.text: The cup, which had been wrapped, came first.
options.feedback: The cup supplies the anchor and the main subject. Paired commas mark the additional comment.

options.text: The cup which had been wrapped came first.
options.feedback: Without commas, the relative can identify which cup. The exercise asks for an added comment.

options.text: Which had been wrapped came first.
options.feedback: That would need a different construction for which. Give came first its own subject.

transfer.prompt: Repair “Which had been wrapped, came first” while keeping the wrapping detail supplementary.
transfer.hint: The sentence needs something that was first. Give it a subject.

options.text: And joins two clauses. Which is a third coordinate.
options.feedback: Large and heavy are two predicative descriptions after was. Neither has a separate clause here.

options.text: And introduces an object. Which modifies only the word heavy.
options.feedback: Which points to the whole description of the crate. Its size and weight together caused the worry.

options.text: And joins two predicative descriptions. Which adds a comment anchored to the state of affairs.
options.feedback: Large and heavy share a predicative function. The source of the worry is the crate’s being large and heavy.

exit.prompt: In “The crate was large and heavy, which worried us”, what do and and which do?
exit.hint: Try “The crate was large” and “The crate was heavy” separately, then ask what worried us.

outcomes.text: Choose an available word order for particles, recipients and extraposed subjects.
Use a cleft to highlight the information a reader is looking for.
Identify which clause becomes passive and choose the required complement form.

teaching.text: Try a short three-turn report: a neutral statement, a question identifying one missing detail and a cleft supplying the answer. This gives the cleft a reason to be there.
In perception examples, have learners underline the matrix verb and circle the lower event. Convert one at a time so that the complement changes are visible.

worked_example.sentence: It would help to close the second valve.

steps.text: Identify the infinitival clause, “to close the second valve”.
Recognise “it” as the extraposition subject and “would” as the finite auxiliary.
Invert “would” and “it” to ask “Would it help to close the second valve?”

key_terms.definition: A construction with it in the usual subject position and a clause later, as in It would help to close the valve.
A construction such as It was Maya who closed the valve, which singles out a value for a role.
A specifying construction such as What helped was closing the valve, with a fused relative as one part.
A construction that can make the affected participant the subject, as in The valve was closed by Maya.

options.text: Might it help to turn the handle?
options.feedback: Might inverts with the extraposition subject it. The infinitival stays after help.

options.text: Might to turn the handle help?
options.feedback: The task starts with extraposition, so keep it in the subject slot and leave the infinitival after help.

options.text: Did it might help to turn the handle?
options.feedback: Might is already an auxiliary. It can move before the subject on its own.

predict.prompt: Turn “It might help to turn the handle” into a direct question.
predict.hint: Keep the infinitival at the end and find the short word in the subject slot.

options.text: It was the alarm that Jo reset.
options.feedback: This cleft foregrounds the alarm. Choose the cleft that puts the person after it was.

options.text: It was Jo who reset the alarm.
options.feedback: The first cleft foregrounds Jo. The other two foreground the thing reset.

options.text: What Jo reset was the alarm.
options.feedback: This focuses the thing Jo reset.

guided.prompt: A reviewer asks “Which person reset the alarm?” Which cleft makes that person the focus?
guided.hint: Look immediately after “It was” in each it-cleft.

options.feedback: Saw remains active. Get splashed makes the lower event passive.

options.text: Maya was seen to close the valve.
options.feedback: Was seen marks the higher passive. Close remains active in the lower infinitival.
Saw is active and the valve undergoes the closing. The task asks you to passivise see.

transfer.prompt: Which edit makes the act of seeing passive, keeping the act of closing active?
transfer.hint: Identify the two events and ask which one the observer is the subject of.

options.text: The former contains a question. The latter uses an overt head with a relative.
options.feedback: An interrogative who clause and a fused relative need not license the same words.

options.text: Called requires a to-infinitival in a specifying clause.
options.feedback: The difference is between an embedded question and a headed relative. Both examples use the same finite verb called.

options.text: Who is a free-standing fused-relative subject in both.
options.feedback: Who starts an embedded interrogative after know. In the other sentence, the one supplies the head of the subject noun phrase.

exit.prompt: Why does “I know who called” work while the course uses “The one who called was Jo” to specify the caller?
exit.hint: Ask whether “who called” stands for a question or whether who modifies the one.

outcomes.text: Trace reflexives and reciprocals to the expressions that license them.
Choose between repeating a noun and using one, a fused head or a demonstrative.
Explain what is recoverable when a verb phrase or other material is left out.

teaching.text: For a reflexive, have the learner point to the subject of the clause containing it before looking at any other name. Then distinguish a reflexive object from an added emphatic reflexive.
Let learners answer the same request in three ways, such as “the red lantern”, “the red one” and “the cheaper”. Ask precisely which word carries the nominal work in each response.
Close by reconstructing a reply word for word. The context supplies a meaning, but a reply such as “neither have I” still needs the auxiliary and polarity required by its own construction.

worked_example.sentence: Jo can check the blue lantern, and so can Mira.

steps.text: Recover “check the blue lantern” after the second “can”.
Find “Mira” as the new subject. The addition is positive, so choose “so”.
Invert the auxiliary and subject in the additive clause.

key_terms.definition: An expression that supplies the interpretation for another expression, as doors supplies the noun understood in the red one.
A form such as herself or themselves. It can point back to a local antecedent or add emphasis in a separate use.
A form such as each other that represents a relation holding in both directions or among members of a group.
A construction where material is unexpressed but can be recovered from the context.

options.feedback: The clause contains the reflexive. Look inside it for the subject, which supplies the antecedent.
Mira supplies the reference for she. The local antecedent of the reflexive is the pronoun she.
She is local to the reflexive. Context can then identify she as Mira.

predict.prompt: In “If she hurts herself, Mira will stop”, which expression is the immediate antecedent of herself?
predict.hint: Start with the subject of hurts. Follow the reference to Mira only after that.

options.feedback: Every requires one in this construction. Each could stand alone.
Every needs an expressed head in this construction. Add the count form one.
Them cannot fill the position after every. In a partitive use “every one of them”.

guided.prompt: After “All the lanterns were tested”, which short subject fits “___ was safe” and expresses every?
guided.hint: Recall what can stand alone in “Each was safe”.

options.feedback: Neither adds a matching negative statement. The first clause is positive here.
The reply adds a different subject affirmatively. Keep can positive and put it before Jo.
The first clause is positive. So adds a positive counterpart with auxiliary–subject order.

transfer.prompt: Which continuation adds Jo to “Mira can lift the crate”?
transfer.hint: Use the same polarity as the first clause and match the auxiliary.

options.feedback: She is already the subject. Read back to the question that was put to her.

options.text: The content of what she could have said, whether it worked
options.feedback: The lexical verb say can leave its complement understood here. She is the overt subject.

options.text: A mandatory direct object after did so
options.feedback: There is no do so here. Didn’t supports the negative, and lexical say can leave its complement understood.

exit.prompt: What is missing in “I asked whether it worked, but she didn’t say”?
exit.hint: Ask what question she could have answered.

outcomes.text: Apply common spelling changes when adding an inflectional suffix.
Distinguish ordinary noun plurals, surname plurals and genitives.
Use sound or clause position to choose between forms such as a and an or am not and aren’t.

teaching.text: Show the bases before presenting their inflections. Contrast “fit” with “visit” so the learner has to use stress as well as letter shape.
Have learners name the number first in a surname example, then add possession as a second operation. The plain plural can stay visible while they choose where the apostrophe goes.

worked_example.sentence: The stage manager has tied the cables, and the Bradys are taking their seats.

steps.text: Recognise “tied” as the past participle selected by “has”. The -ing form would be “tying”.
Read “the Bradys” as the plain plural of the surname.
If the seats belong to the family, write “the Bradys’ seats”.

key_terms.definition: A form change that marks a grammatical distinction such as past tense or plural.
The form to which a suffix is attached, such as fit in fitted.
A form that marks a relation such as possession, as in the guests’ coats.

options.feedback: Doubling adds one t to fit. This spelling adds two.
The stressed one-syllable base fit doubles its final consonant before -ing.
Fit keeps its short stressed vowel and doubles its t before -ing.

predict.prompt: Which form of fit completes “The crew is ___ the latch”?
predict.hint: Start from the base fit and check the last two letters.

options.feedback: Form the plural Bradys first, then mark the genitive after the plural s.
Brady’s is singular genitive. Add the plural first to refer to the family.
The plural of the family name is Bradys. Keep y before the ending.

guided.prompt: Write the genitive for the seats assigned to the Brady family as a group.
guided.hint: Write the family’s plain plural first.

options.feedback: Sang is the past tense, and perfect have selects the past participle sung.
Sung is the participle, so it belongs after have. Begin with the past sang.
Sing uses irregular past and participial forms, sang and sung.

transfer.prompt: Which forms complete “I ___ yesterday. I’ve ___ today” for sing?
transfer.hint: The blank after have needs a participle.

options.feedback: Am not fits. Hour begins with a vowel sound, so change the article.
Aren’t I is ordinary in the inverted question, but I aren’t is not the corresponding standard statement. Hour needs an.
The uninverted statement uses am not, and hour starts with a vowel sound.

exit.prompt: Choose the ordinary statement and article in “I ___ sure we have ___ hour to wait.”
exit.hint: Say hour aloud and compare the negative question with the negative statement.

outcomes.text: Distinguish a new word built from a base from an inflected form of an existing word.
Build and spell familiar compounds, derivatives and inhabitant names.
Read a composite numeral or fraction from the inside out.

teaching.text: Keep a number constant across phrases, such as “four nights” and “a four-night stay”. Ask where the count is expressed in each.
Build a composite numeral in stages. Read the multiplier with its power word, then say what is added. That makes the uninflected power word visible.

worked_example.sentence: Around three fifths of the visitors chose the two-day tour.

steps.text: Read “three fifths” as a numerator followed by the plural denominator.
Keep “day” singular inside the measure modifier “two-day”.
Compare “the tour lasts two days”, where “days” heads the measure phrase itself.

key_terms.definition: Word formation that creates a new word from a base, as in drive and driver.
A word formed from two or more bases, as in passer-by.
The part giving the number of hundreds, thousands or other powers in a composite numeral.

options.text: a two-days tour / a two-bedroomed flat
options.feedback: The descriptive compound is right. Keep day singular inside the measure modifier.

options.text: a two-day tour / a two-bedroomed flat
options.feedback: Day stays singular in the measure compound. The -ed formation is built with the uninflected noun bedroom.

options.text: a two-days tour / a two-bedroomsed flat
options.feedback: Remove the plural forms from day and bedroom in these formations.

predict.prompt: Which pair uses singular nouns inside both measure or descriptive formations?
predict.hint: In both modifiers, the number already tells you how many.

options.feedback: The verb commit has final stress. Double t in committal. The driver spelling is right.
Committal works. Before -er, drive drops the final e.
Commit doubles t before the suffix in committal. Drive drops silent e before -er.

guided.prompt: Which pair shows the ordinary spelling of both derivatives?
guided.hint: Check the stress of commit and the silent e in drive.

options.text: two thousands one hundred and three
options.feedback: Thousand stays uninflected after its multiplier, two.

options.text: two thousand one hundred and three
options.feedback: Both power words remain uninflected. One hundred supplies the hundreds portion.

options.text: two thousand one hundreds and three
options.feedback: The hundreds portion of the numeral uses singular-looking hundred.

transfer.prompt: Which is the ordinary composite numeral for 2,103 in the style that says and before the final three?
transfer.hint: Read the thousands portion, then the hundreds portion, then the addition.

options.text: Fifths is the fraction’s head, counted by the numerator.
options.feedback: The denominator is the noun-like head. Its number depends on the numerator.

options.text: Three always makes the following word an ordinal.
options.feedback: Three is the numerator. It counts the denominator, whose spelling shows the ordinal and plural.

options.text: Only the numerator can show number.
options.feedback: Number shows on the denominator here. The numerator supplies the count.

exit.prompt: Why is fifths plural in “three fifths” but not in “one fifth”?
exit.hint: In a fraction, ask which word is being counted.

outcomes.text: Choose punctuation from the structure of the whole written sentence.
Set off supplements, parenthetical material and direct speech using a consistent style.
Handle apostrophes, hyphens and terminal punctuation in common editing cases.

teaching.text: Have the learner read the matrix clause with the quotation temporarily replaced by “this”. Then look inside the quote to determine which terminal belongs to its own sentence.
When commas surround added material, try removing the entire span. The surrounding clause should retain its expected subject and predicate.

worked_example.sentence: “Mara,” Jo asked, “is the hall open?”

steps.text: Read the quoted speech as the single question “Mara, is the hall open?”
Keep the comma marking the vocative and set off the reporting interruption according to the quotation style.
Put the question mark at the end of the quoted question, which also ends the matrix sentence.

key_terms.definition: A mark such as a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark that can end a written sentence.
An expression naming the person being addressed, as in Jo, close the door.
An expression such as however that links a clause’s meaning to surrounding text.
The larger sentence containing an embedded question, quotation or other construction.

options.text: Mara asked what time the doors open.
options.feedback: Asked appears in ordinary declarative order here. The embedded question cannot turn the whole line into a direct question.

options.text: Did Mara ask what time the doors open?
options.feedback: The main clause did Mara ask is interrogative. The embedded question stays the same.

options.text: Neither main sentence is a question.
options.feedback: The version starting “Did Mara ask” has direct-question inversion in its outer clause.

predict.prompt: Which main sentence is a question even though both contain “what time the doors open”?
predict.hint: Read the outer clause on its own before looking at the embedded question.

options.text: The hall, was shut. However the courtyard, was open.
options.feedback: The hall is the subject of was shut and takes no delimiting comma there. Set off however in the second sentence.

options.text: The hall was shut, however, the courtyard was open.
options.feedback: However does not give a comma extra force. Put a full stop or semicolon at the main clause boundary.

options.text: The hall was shut. However, the courtyard was open.
options.feedback: Use a sentence boundary before the connective. The comma after however separates it from its clause.

guided.prompt: Which edit gives two clear independent clauses in ordinary edited prose?
guided.hint: Check whether however joins two complete statements.

options.feedback: A lone opening comma would leave the end of the interruption unmarked.
A lone closing comma would leave the start of the interruption unmarked.
The added comment is enclosed on both sides. The base clause is The side gate was locked.

transfer.prompt: Where are the commas needed in “The side gate as you know was locked”?
transfer.hint: Try removing the whole interposed comment, then put it back.

options.feedback: That is enough for a statement about the city. The larger question still needs its question mark.
The abbreviation retains its stop, and the whole question has its own question mark.
The whole line asks a question. Use a question mark after the abbreviation’s stop.

exit.prompt: Complete the direct question “Did she say the venue was in Washington, ___”
exit.hint: The city abbreviation has its own punctuation. What is the whole sentence doing?
